Qualifying CCPCs and ECPCs earn a 35% refundable investment tax credit on up to $6 million of qualified expenditures, and compute-heavy software teams may claim cloud costs under the Traditional Method.

Qualifying CCPCs and ECPCs earn a 35% refundable investment tax credit on up to $6 million of qualified expenditures, and compute-heavy software teams may claim cloud costs under the Traditional Method.
Executive Overview of the Canadian R&D Tax Landscape

Canada operates one of the most comprehensive fiscal support architectures for industrial research and technological innovation among major developed economies, anchored federally by the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program. Administered jointly by the Department of Finance Canada—which retains exclusive purview over statutory policy and legislative design—and the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA)—which executes technical eligibility assessments, financial audits, and credit disbursements—the SR&ED framework supports more than 22,000 claimant enterprises nationwide, including approximately 4,000 corporations operating within the province of Quebec.

Between 2024 and 2026, the federal SR&ED architecture underwent its most consequential statutory overhaul in over a decade. Following a two-phase national consultation initiated by the Department of Finance Canada on January 31, 2024—the first phase closing on April 15, 2024, and the second phase extending to May 27, 2024—and reinforced in Budget 2024 (Fairness for Every Generation) tabled on April 16, 2024, the federal government committed $600 million over four years commencing in 2025, with $150 million per year in ongoing annual fiscal support, to modernize the incentive structure. While initial policy proposals tabled in the December 16, 2024 Fall Economic Statement (FES 2024) contemplated raising the enhanced expenditure limit from $3 million to $4.5 million, subsequent legislative refinements introduced through the November 4, 2025 federal budget culminated in the enactment of Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1, S.C. 2026, c. 3), a 638-page omnibus statute that received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026.

Enacted into law by Bill C-15 and applying retroactively to taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024, the modernized statutory regime introduces four structural transformations to the Income Tax Act (R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.)) and the Income Tax Regulations (C.R.C., c. 945). First, the legislation doubles the enhanced expenditure limit: the annual qualified expenditure ceiling eligible for the enhanced 35% Investment Tax Credit (ITC) increased from the historical $3 million limit to a finalized $6 million limit, enabling qualifying corporations to generate up to $2.1 million in refundable federal tax credits annually. Second, the reform expands refundable credit eligibility to public companies: access to the enhanced 35% refundable ITC—historically restricted exclusively to Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs)—was extended to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) on up to $6 million of qualified SR&ED expenditures. Third, the statutory amendments expand and flexibilize the phase-out thresholds: the prior-year taxable capital phase-out corridor governing the enhanced expenditure limit was raised from the legacy $10 million–$50 million range to $15 million–$75 million, while CCPCs gained the statutory right to elect to calculate their expenditure limit phase-out using a three-year average gross revenue test ($15 million–$75 million) rather than taxable capital, a gross revenue metric that is mandatory for ECPCs. Fourth, Bill C-15 executes a full reinstatement of capital and lease expenditures: reversing the legislative repeal enacted in 2012 (which had eliminated capital expenditure eligibility effective in 2014), the law restores both section 37 income deduction pool eligibility and subsection 127(9) ITC eligibility for depreciable capital property acquired, and lease costs first becoming payable, on or after December 16, 2024.

body.text: The structural interplay between these legislative amendments alters corporate capital allocation across Canada's technology, biomanufacturing, clean technology, electric vehicle manufacturing, and microelectronics sectors. Previously, capital-intensive R&D enterprises—such as semiconductor fabrication facilities, clean-tech hardware developers, and biotechnology firms—suffered a double fiscal penalty: their balance-sheet equipment investments were excluded from SR&ED claim pools post-2012/2014, while the equity and debt raised to finance those very capital assets inflated their taxable capital employed in Canada above $10 million, prematurely eroding their access to the 35% refundable credit. By simultaneously restoring capital expenditure eligibility, raising the phase-out corridor to $15 million–$75 million, and permitting CCPCs to substitute a three-year gross revenue averaging metric for taxable capital, Bill C-15 eliminates the structural disincentive against domestic capital formation and domestic public listings on exchanges such as the Toronto Stock Exchange (TSX).
Statutory and Legislative Architecture of the Federal SR&ED Program
Core Provisions of the Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations

The legal foundation of the federal SR&ED tax incentive rests on a two-stage statutory mechanism within the Income Tax Act that separates the deduction of research expenditures from the generation of investment tax credits. At the threshold of the regime, subsection 248(1) establishes the substantive legal definition of qualifying scientific or technological activity, bifurcating eligible work into core research categories—basic research, applied research, and experimental development—and enumerated categories of directly commensurate support work. Once work satisfies subsection 248(1), section 37 governs the accumulation and deduction of current and, for property acquired on or after December 16, 2024, capital expenditures incurred by a taxpayer in respect of SR&ED carried on in Canada. Expenditures pooled under subsection 37(1) may be deducted in full in computing net business income for the current taxation year to eliminate current tax liability, or carried forward indefinitely inside the section 37 expenditure pool to offset business income in future taxation years.

While section 37 generally enforces a strict territoriality principle requiring SR&ED to be carried on within Canada, subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5) provide a tightly circumscribed exception for permissible foreign salaries. Under subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5), a taxpayer may include salaries or wages paid to Canadian-resident employees performing SR&ED work outside Canada, provided the foreign activity is undertaken solely in support of SR&ED carried on in Canada and the included foreign salaries do not exceed 10% of the total salaries and wages directly attributable to SR&ED carried on in Canada during the taxation year. Compliance with the expenditure pool rules is further policed by subsection 78(4), which excludes from current-year SR&ED expenditure pools any salary, wages, or other remuneration accrued at year-end that remains unpaid on the day that is 180 days after the end of the taxation year in which the expense was incurred, deferring its statutory inclusion until the subsequent taxation year in which the amount is actually paid.

The transition from the section 37 deduction pool to tax credit generation is governed by subsection 127(9), which defines both "qualified expenditure" and "investment tax credit". Qualified expenditures under subsection 127(9) encompass current and eligible capital SR&ED expenditures, 80% of eligible arm's-length Canadian contract payments, and—where elected by the taxpayer on Form T661—the notional Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) for overhead. Unused non-refundable SR&ED ITCs earned under subsection 127(9) may be carried back 3 taxation years and carried forward up to 20 taxation years to offset Part I federal income tax otherwise payable. For domestic growth enterprises, subsections 127(10.1) through 127(10.6) establish the additional 20% enhanced ITC—bringing the base 15% rate to 35%—for qualifying CCPCs and ECPCs up to their annual expenditure limit, and mandate that associated corporations allocate the $6 million expenditure limit amongst themselves via a prescribed agreement filed under subsection 127(10.3). In turn, section 127.1 governs the conversion of unused SR&ED ITCs into cash refunds for qualifying CCPCs, ECPCs, and unincorporated taxpayers.

Both the section 37 deduction pool and the subsection 127(9) credit calculation are subject to an uncompromising procedural gatekeeper: subsection 37(11) and paragraph (m) of the definition of "investment tax credit" in subsection 127(9) mandate that no amount may be included in the deductible pool or the ITC calculation unless the taxpayer files the prescribed forms (Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 or Form T2038(IND)) containing prescribed information in respect of the expenditure on or before the day that is 12 months after the taxpayer's filing-due date for the taxation year, yielding a total reporting window of 18 months from the end of a corporate taxation year under paragraph 150(1)(a). Finally, section 2900 of the Income Tax Regulations prescribes the granular regulatory mechanics for qualifying scientific work, expenditures directly attributable to the provision of premises, facilities or equipment under subsection 2900(3), the calculation of the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount under subsection 2900(4), specified employee proxy salary caps under subsections 2900(7) and 2900(8), and exclusions from the proxy salary base under subsection 2900(9).
Pool Recapture and Government Assistance Adjustments

To prevent double-dipping between tax deductions, grants, and investment tax credits, the Income Tax Act enforces an automatic pool reduction mechanism. Under subsection 37(1) and subsection 127(9), both the section 37 deductible SR&ED expenditure pool and the current-year qualified expenditures for ITC calculation must be reduced by the amount of any government assistance or non-government assistance—including provincial R&D tax credits such as the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit, the Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit, the Quebec CRIC, and historic Alberta SR&ED tax credits, as well as direct federal innovation grants—that the taxpayer has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive in respect of the SR&ED expenditures.

Furthermore, federal SR&ED ITCs claimed in a taxation year, whether refunded in cash or applied to reduce Part I tax otherwise payable, are included in the taxpayer's taxable income or deducted from the section 37 expenditure pool in the subsequent taxation year, ensuring that a taxpayer does not claim both an income tax deduction and a tax credit on the exact same slice of expenditure. Conversely, where a corporation disposes of SR&ED property—including newly restored capital equipment or experimental prototypes—or converts the asset to commercial use within the statutory recapture period, the SR&ED ITC previously claimed on that asset is subject to ITC recapture calculated on Schedule T2SCH31, which directly creates or increases Part I federal tax otherwise payable.
Complementary Innovation Tax Measures Enacted Alongside SR&ED Modernization

The 2024–2026 federal fiscal cycle paired SR&ED reform with broader capital cost allowance (CCA), sovereign infrastructure, and intellectual property retention measures aimed at scaling domestic technological capacity. Introduced in Budget 2024 and enacted via Bill C-15, an immediate expensing incentive allows Canadian businesses to immediately write off 100% of the capital cost of eligible patents (or rights to use patented information), data network infrastructure equipment, and general-purpose electronic data processing equipment and computers acquired on or after April 16, 2024, and becoming available for use before January 1, 2027. Extending beyond this targeted write-off, FES 2024 proposed and Bill C-15 enacted on March 26, 2026, the reinstatement of the Accelerated Investment Incentive for a five-year window commencing January 1, 2025, for qualifying depreciable capital assets becoming available for use before 2030, enabling accelerated upfront depreciation rather than standard declining-balance CCA deductions.

To reinforce computational infrastructure and domestic intellectual property ownership, Budget 2024 also allocated $2.4 billion toward artificial intelligence capacity—comprising $2 billion to establish an AI Compute Access Fund and Canadian AI Sovereign Compute Strategy, $200 million to accelerate AI adoption and commercialization in key sectors, $100 million for the National Research Council's (NRC) AI Assist Program supporting Canadian SMEs, and $50 million for workforce transition—alongside $14.5 million over two years for Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada's (ISED) Innovation Asset Collective and ongoing funding for the $2 billion Global Innovation Clusters. Concurrently, following national consultations on intellectual property retention that closed on April 15, 2024, FES 2024 formally announced the federal government's intention to legislate a Canadian patent box regime designed to apply a reduced corporate income tax rate to income derived from patents and intellectual property developed in Canada.
Federal SR&ED Tax Credit Rates, Thresholds, and Refundability Mechanics
The Bifurcated Rate Structure: 35% Enhanced Rate vs. 15% Basic Rate

The financial value of an SR&ED claim depends primarily on the corporate classification of the claimant and its position relative to the statutory expenditure limit. Following the Royal Assent of Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026, claimants fall into four distinct statutory classifications for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024, with qualifying CCPCs and ECPCs earning the enhanced 35% refundable rate on up to $6 million of qualified expenditures and 15% on excess expenditures, while other corporations and unincorporated entities earn the basic 15% rate.

body.text: Qualifying Criteria for Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs)

Historically, the moment a high-growth Canadian private technology, clean-tech, or life-sciences company completed an initial public offering (IPO) or reverse takeover (RTO) on a designated stock exchange such as the TSX, NASDAQ, or NYSE, it ceased to qualify as a CCPC. Consequently, its federal SR&ED ITC rate immediately plunged from 35% (100% refundable) to 15% (0% refundable), depriving pre-profit public R&D companies of critical non-dilutive working capital at the precise stage when scaling expenditures peaked.

To rectify this structural penalty, Bill C-15 introduced the statutory category of the Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC) for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024. To qualify as an ECPC for a given taxation year, a corporation must satisfy four cumulative conditions throughout the taxation year. First, the entity must be a taxable Canadian corporation that is resident in Canada. Second, the corporation must maintain public corporation status—meaning it has a class of shares listed on a designated Canadian or foreign stock exchange, has validly elected to be a public corporation, or has been designated as a public corporation by the Minister of National Revenue—and consequently is not a CCPC. Third, the corporation must not be controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever, by one or more non-resident persons. Fourth, the corporation must satisfy the active business and gross revenue criteria, whereby eligibility for the $6 million enhanced expenditure limit phases out based on the corporation's average gross revenue over the three preceding taxation years.
Mathematical Formulation of the Expenditure Limit Phase-Out

For taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024, the base enhanced expenditure limit for an associated corporate group is $6,000,000. This $6,000,000 limit is reduced on a straight-line basis when the corporation's (and its associated corporations') prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada—or, where elected by a CCPC or mandated for an ECPC, its three-year average gross revenue—falls between $15,000,000 and $75,000,000.

Expressed mathematically, for a CCPC electing the taxable capital method or an ECPC/CCPC utilizing the three-year average gross revenue metric (X), the adjusted annual expenditure limit (L) is calculated according to the linear reduction formula:

Within this statutory equation, the variable X represents either the total taxable capital employed in Canada of the corporation and all associated corporations for the immediately preceding taxation year, or the average of the gross revenues of the corporation and its associated corporate group over the three preceding taxation years. Consequently, every $10 of prior-year taxable capital or three-year average gross revenue above the $15,000,000 floor reduces the $6,000,000 expenditure limit by $1.00. When X reaches or exceeds $75,000,000, the enhanced expenditure limit L is reduced to nil ($0), and all qualified SR&ED expenditures of the corporation revert to the basic 15% non-refundable ITC rate. For associated corporate groups, failure to execute and file the prescribed allocation agreement under subsection 127(10.3) before claiming credits exposes the group to assessment adjustments when the combined claim exceeds the shared $6,000,000 ceiling.
Qualifying SR&ED Expenditures (QREs) and Calculation Methods

Under section 37 and subsection 127(9) of the Income Tax Act, only specific categories of expenditures directly attributable to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada qualify for tax deduction and ITC generation.
Salaries and Wages and Specified Employee Restrictions

Salaries and wages paid to employees directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada constitute the primary expenditure base for most claimants. Eligible labour encompasses hands-on experimentation, testing, prototype construction, direct technical supervision, and enumerated support activities under subsection 248(1), whereas routine design iteration and commercial administration do not qualify regardless of the hours absorbed.

However, the Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations impose stringent anti-avoidance caps on specified employees—broadly defined as employees who are specified shareholders owning, directly or indirectly, at any time in the year, 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the corporation or a related corporation, or who do not deal at arm's length with the employer. First, with respect to direct SR&ED salary inclusion in the expenditure pool, the maximum direct SR&ED salary or wages claimable for a specified employee is capped at 5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) determined for purposes of the Canada Pension Plan for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends, prorated by the number of days of employment in the taxation year, and bonuses or remuneration based on profits paid to specified employees are strictly excluded.

Second, when calculating the salary base to which the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) applies under the proxy overhead method, subsections 2900(7), 2900(8), and 2900(9) of the Income Tax Regulations enforce an even tighter restriction. Specifically, Regulation 2900(7) restricts the amount that a claimant can include in the proxy salary base for a specified employee to the lesser of two statutory ceilings: first, 75% of the specified employee's total salary or wages for the year (combining both SR&ED and non-SR&ED duties, but excluding bonuses, remuneration based on profits, taxable benefits, and prior-year unpaid salary or wages paid in the year pursuant to Regulation 2900(9)); or second, 2.5 times the YMPE for the calendar year in which the claimant's taxation year ends, prorated for the number of days of employment in the year according to the regulatory formula:

In this regulatory formula under subsection 2900(7), A is the YMPE for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends, and B is the number of days in the taxation year that the claimant employed the individual, with no proration permitted for any period during the year in which the employee was not a specified employee. Furthermore, where a specified employee of a corporation is also employed by an associated corporation, additional allocation rules under subsection 2900(8) apply across the associated group.
Overhead Costing: Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) vs. Traditional Method

A claimant must elect on Line 160 of Form T661 whether to calculate SR&ED overhead using the Prescribed Proxy Amount (Proxy Method) or the Traditional Method. Under section 37 of the Income Tax Act, this election is made on the first Form T661 filed for the taxation year and is irrevocable for that taxation year.

body.text: A recurring compliance error encountered during CRA financial reviews involves claimants or non-specialist preparers applying the obsolete 65% proxy rate—which has not applied since 2012, having dropped to 60% in 2013 and 55% from 2014 onward under subsection 2900(4) of the Income Tax Regulations—thereby overstating the credit by ten percentage points on every claim. Equally problematic is the attempt to claim cloud computing infrastructure or specialized software subscriptions as separate line items while simultaneously electing the 55% Proxy Method on Line 160. Because the 55% PPA under Regulation 2900(4) is a notional statutory substitute representing overhead of every kind, claiming software subscriptions or cloud compute separately under the proxy method constitutes double counting. Conversely, for artificial intelligence and data analytics enterprises whose dedicated cloud compute and development software fees exceed 55% of their eligible technical salary base—for instance, where a team of five engineers earning $600,000 in eligible salary would generate $330,000 of notional proxy overhead, but incurs higher actual incremental compute costs—deliberately electing the Traditional Method on Line 160 allows both the actual overhead and cloud spend to be itemized into the section 37 pool and ITC base.
Subcontractors, Third-Party Payments, and Materials

Payments made to arm's-length Canadian contractors or subcontractors performing SR&ED work on behalf of the claimant in Canada are eligible for inclusion in the section 37 deductible expenditure pool, but only 80% of the eligible contract payment qualifies as a "qualified expenditure" under subsection 127(9) for the purpose of calculating the SR&ED investment tax credit. To substantiate arm's-length contractor claims during a CRA audit, the claimant must retain statements of work and itemized invoices specifically identifying the eligible SR&ED activities performed in Canada on the claimant's behalf.

With respect to physical inputs, the cost of materials is fully includable in both the section 37 pool and the subsection 127(9) qualified expenditure base only where the materials are directly consumed (rendered unusable or destroyed during experimental trials) or transformed (physically integrated into an experimental prototype or pilot build) in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada. General office and studio supplies do not qualify as SR&ED materials, and where a claimant elects the proxy method, such general supplies are already subsumed inside the 55% PPA under Regulation 2900(4). Claimants must maintain purchase invoices alongside build logs demonstrating which experimental trial or prototype consumed or transformed each material lot.
Reinstatement of Capital Expenditures and Lease Costs (Post-December 15, 2024)

One of the most consequential technical reforms enacted by Bill C-15 (S.C. 2026, c. 3) on March 26, 2026, is the full reinstatement of capital expenditures and SR&ED lease expenditures for property acquired—or rental/lease costs that first become payable—on or after December 16, 2024. Reversing the policy repeal that had been in place since 2012/2014, the restored rules revert to the pre-2014 statutory standard under section 37, subsection 127(9), and Regulation 2900(3).

Under the restored capital expenditure rules, depreciable property acquired on or after December 16, 2024, and becoming available for use after that date qualifies for both section 37 deduction and subsection 127(9) ITC calculation if the equipment and machinery are used all or substantially all—defined as 90% or more of their operating time—for SR&ED in Canada, or if all or substantially all of their monetary value is consumed in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada. Qualifying capital expenditures include R&D laboratory and testing equipment, prototyping machinery, custom tooling and moulds, specialized measurement tools and devices, infrastructure primarily used for experimentation, and computers and software bought outright or fees for software and cloud space used for development. While a qualifying CCPC within its $6 million expenditure limit receives 100% refundability on its 35% enhanced ITC earned on current expenditures, the refundable share of a CCPC's enhanced 35% SR&ED credit earned on qualifying capital expenditures up to the expenditure limit is 40%. Concurrently, the CRA updated its administrative SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy (including Appendix B explaining the legislative changes) to govern SR&ED lease expenditures incurred after December 15, 2024.
Scientific Eligibility Criteria and Foundational Jurisprudence
Statutory Definition under Subsection 248(1)

Regardless of the quantum of financial expenditure, no SR&ED claim can succeed unless the underlying technical activity satisfies the statutory definition of "scientific research and experimental development" in subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act. Subsection 248(1) requires a systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis, categorizing eligible primary research into basic research, applied research, and experimental development undertaken to achieve a technological advancement. Alongside these core research categories, subsection 248(1) permits supporting work—such as engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, and testing—only to the extent that such activities are commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of the core basic research, applied research, or experimental development. Conversely, routine engineering, standard procedures, commercial production, quality control, and routine design iteration are statutorily excluded from SR&ED eligibility.
The Canonical Five Questions: Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen

Although the CRA updated its administrative guidance to present two consolidated requirements—referred to as the "Why" and the "How"—to provide a common language for claimants and CRA officials when discussing eligibility, the CRA explicitly confirms in its Brief History of Guidance on the Eligibility of Work that both the two administrative requirements and the classic five judicial questions are derived directly from the statutory definition of SR&ED in subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act, which did not change. In the Tax Court of Canada and the Federal Court of Appeal, the controlling legal test remains the five criteria articulated by the Tax Court of Canada in the foundational decision Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, 1998 CarswellNat 696, 98 DTC 1839 (Docket: 97-531-IT-G, decided May 1, 1998).

First, the court asks whether there was a technological risk or uncertainty which could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedure. If the resolution of a technical problem is achievable by applying standard practices or routine engineering known to competent professionals in the field, no qualifying technological uncertainty exists. Second, the court examines whether the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulated hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty. Third, the inquiry evaluates whether the procedures adopted accorded with the total discipline of the scientific method, including the systematic formulation, testing, and modification of those hypotheses through experiment or analysis. Fourth, the court determines whether the process resulted in a technological advancement—that is to say, an advancement in the general technological understanding. Fifth, the court verifies whether the taxpayer kept a detailed contemporaneous record of the hypotheses, tests, and results as the work progressed.
Evolution of Appellate and Trial Jurisprudence

Subsequent decisions of the Tax Court of Canada and the Federal Court of Appeal have reinforced and refined the application of Northwest Hydraulic across diverse industrial, manufacturing, and food-science contexts, establishing binding parameters for audit defence and tax litigation.

body.text: The contrast between the taxpayer defeat in Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. (decided May 11, 2011, by Justice Steven K. D'Arcy) and the taxpayer victory in Manning Canning Kitchens Inc. v. The King (decided by Justice Bodie) demonstrates the critical importance of evidentiary presentation in SR&ED appeals. In Canadian tax litigation, the Crown is not required to call its own CRA science auditors as witnesses if the appellant fails to discharge its evidentiary burden. In Jentel, the taxpayer relied heavily on a Statement of Agreed Facts, which constrained the factual record before the trial judge, and failed to prove how standard engineering practices fell short. Conversely, in Manning Canning Kitchens, the appellant sought to control microbial growth in a vinegar-based drink to achieve room-temperature shelf stability. Although the Minister denied the claim on the grounds that the taxpayer experimented with preservatives already known to competent professionals—specifically potassium sorbate, sodium benzoate, and ultimately Chiber—Justice Bodie ruled that technological uncertainty existed because those publicly available solutions had never been proven in that specific product context, and confirmed that the appellant's progressive test records satisfied all five Northwest Hydraulic questions.
Administrative Governance, Filing Procedures, and Audit Defence
Prescribed Forms and the Structure of Form T661

To claim SR&ED tax incentives federally, a taxpayer must file a coordinated set of prescribed tax forms with the Canada Revenue Agency. Every claimant must complete Form T661 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim), which captures project-by-project technical descriptions, itemizes eligible SR&ED expenditures, records the irrevocable Line 160 overhead election between the proxy and traditional methods, and discloses claim preparer billing information. Following the Royal Assent of Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026, the 2026 version of Form T661 incorporates the legislative amendments governing restored capital expenditures, ECPC eligibility, and the $6 million expenditure limit. Alongside Form T661, corporate claimants must file Schedule T2SCH31 (Investment Tax Credit – Corporations) to calculate the 35% enhanced or 15% basic SR&ED ITC, compute the expenditure limit and associated-group phase-out, report any ITC recapture, and coordinate with other federal business tax credits such as the Atlantic Investment Tax Credit (AITC), the Clean Technology ITC (Form T2SCH75), the Clean Electricity ITC (claimed at line 185 of Schedule 31), and the Carbon Capture, Utilization, and Storage (CCUS) ITC. Unincorporated individuals and qualifying trusts claim their SR&ED ITC using Form T2038(IND) (Investment Tax Credit (Individuals)) rather than Schedule T2SCH31.

Within Part 2 of Form T661 (Project Data), the technical project description is organized around three specific lines—Lines 242, 244, and 246—that bridge the CRA's administrative "Why and How" requirements with the five questions of Northwest Hydraulic. On Line 242, the claimant must define the specific scientific or technological obstacles or uncertainties that could not be resolved through standard procedures or routine engineering. On Line 244, the claimant must detail the systematic investigation performed in the taxation year to overcome those uncertainties, documenting the specific hypotheses formulated, the experimental tests or analyses conducted, and the results observed as the work progressed. Finally, on Line 246, the claimant must articulate the scientific or technological advancements achieved or sought as a result of the work described on Line 244, establishing how the targeted knowledge exceeded the existing technological baseline.
The Absolute 18-Month Statutory Filing Deadline

A rigid procedural rule in Canadian R&D tax administration is the separation between the standard corporate income tax return filing period and the absolute statutory bar for SR&ED claims. Under paragraph 150(1)(a) of the Income Tax Act, a Canadian corporation is required to file its T2 corporate income tax return within 6 months after the end of its taxation year, and filing Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 together with the T2 return at the six-month mark is recommended to expedite refund processing.

However, under subsection 37(11) and paragraph (m) of the definition of "investment tax credit" in subsection 127(9), the statutory reporting deadline to submit Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 containing prescribed information for an expenditure is 12 months after the corporation's filing-due date under paragraph 150(1)(a)—establishing a hard statutory deadline of exactly 18 months from the end of the taxation year. Critically, under subsection 220(2.2) of the Income Tax Act, there is no statutory mechanism or ministerial discretion to extend or waive this 18-month reporting deadline. Any expenditure that is late-filed or omitted after the 18-month mark ceases to qualify as an SR&ED expenditure by operation of law.
Pre-Claim Approval and Claim Preparer Penalties

To provide upfront eligibility certainty prior to filing a tax return, the CRA administers a formal Pre-Claim Approval process for qualifying businesses. To be eligible to apply for SR&ED Pre-Claim Approval, an applicant corporation must have gross business income below $25 million.

Simultaneously, the Income Tax Act enforces strict transparency regarding external consultants and tax advisors who prepare SR&ED submissions. Under subsection 162(5.1) of the Income Tax Act, complete and accurate information identifying any SR&ED claim preparer and their fee arrangement (including contingency fees) must be reported on Form T661. Where required SR&ED claim preparer information is missing, incomplete, or false, subsection 162(5.1) imposes a mandatory $1,000 penalty per SR&ED claim, for which the corporate claimant and the claim preparer are jointly and severally liable.
Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes

Canada's provinces and territories supplement the federal SR&ED program with harmonized or autonomous R&D tax incentives. Because all provincial and territorial R&D tax credits constitute "government assistance" under subsection 127(9) of the federal Income Tax Act, every dollar of provincial R&D tax credit earned reduces both the federal section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures and the federal qualified SR&ED expenditures on which the 35% or 15% federal ITC is computed.

body.text: Detailed Analysis of Major Provincial Regimes
Ontario: OITC, ORDTC, and OBRITC Stacking Mechanics

Corporations with a permanent establishment in Ontario that carry out SR&ED in the province can access three harmonized tax credits administered by the Canada Revenue Agency since December 31, 2008. First, the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC) provides an 8% fully refundable tax credit for taxation years starting after May 31, 2016 (reduced from 10% for taxation years ending before June 1, 2016) on qualified SR&ED expenditures carried on in Ontario up to an annual expenditure limit of $3,000,000. The $3,000,000 OITC expenditure limit phases out when the corporation's taxable income for its preceding taxation year exceeds $500,000 and is eliminated at $800,000, or when prior-year taxable paid-up capital exceeds $25,000,000 and is eliminated at $50,000,000. Because any OITC in excess of tax otherwise payable is refunded directly in cash, carryback and carryforward rules do not apply, and no recapture applies to the OITC.

Second, the Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC) provides a 3.5% non-refundable tax credit for taxation years starting after May 31, 2016 (reduced from 4.5% prior to June 1, 2016) on eligible SR&ED expenditures carried out in Ontario. Third, the Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC) is fully refundable at a rate of 20% of qualified expenditures incurred under eligible research institute contracts in Ontario, subject to a $20,000,000 annual expenditure cap. Importantly, qualified expenditures for the OITC are reduced by government and non-government assistance, but are not reduced by the OITC itself, the OBRITC, the ORDTC, or the federal SR&ED ITC. However, because the OITC and ORDTC constitute government assistance for federal purposes and therefore reduce the federal pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures and federal qualified expenditures, Ontario legislation permits a corporation to waive the tax credit, or any portion thereof, by delivering a written waiver with its corporate tax return filed on or before six months after its taxation year-end, or on an amended return for that year.
Quebec: Transition to the Unified CRIC Regime (2025–2026)

Quebec administers an independent corporate tax system through Revenu Québec, supporting approximately 4,000 R&D-active companies in the province. While the Quebec government sought $2.9 billion in broader fiscal savings over five years during its recent budget cycle, it elected not to drain overall support for the R&D tax credit system. Instead, for all taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, Quebec introduced a consolidated Tax Credit for R&D and Pre-Commercialization (CRIC), which replaces the legacy R&D salary and subcontracting tax credit (Form RD-1029.7) and related consortium credits, and is claimed on prescribed Revenu Québec Form RD-1029.8.CR.

Under the CRIC architecture, the eligible cost base is significantly broadened beyond traditional R&D to encompass both scientific research and experimental development and pre-commercialization activities. In calculating the credit, corporate claimants—as well as corporate members of a partnership receiving an RL-15 slip (reported on line 210 of Form RD-1029.7 under the legacy filing instructions and governed by the Guide to Filing the Partnership Information Return, TP-600-G-V)—must account for the statutory exclusion threshold before applying the applicable Quebec refundable tax credit rate.
Alberta: The Innovation Employment Grant (IEG)

Overseen by the Ministry of Technology and Innovation and delivered through the corporate income tax system by Alberta Tax and Revenue Administration (TRA), the Alberta Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) replaced the former Alberta SR&ED tax credit for eligible expenditures incurred in Alberta after December 31, 2020. Codified in sections 26.95 to 26.99 of the Alberta Corporate Tax Act and detailed in Information Circular IEG-1 and the Guide to Claiming the Alberta Innovation Employment Grant, the IEG provides qualified corporations with a two-tier refundable grant of up to 20% toward qualifying R&D expenditures carried out in Alberta that match those qualifying for the federal SR&ED program (including the Alberta proxy amount, where applicable).

Specifically, the IEG provides an 8% payment for eligible R&D spending carried out in Alberta up to the corporation's base level of spending, and an enhanced 20% payment for eligible R&D spending that exceeds the corporation's base spending level. A corporation's base level of spending is determined by calculating the corporation's average qualifying Alberta R&D spending over the previous two taxation years. Consequently, a newly established R&D performer in Alberta with $0 of spending over the prior two years earns the full 20% enhanced rate across its entire eligible expenditure base up to the statutory cap. The IEG provides benefits on up to $4,000,000 in annual R&D spending, yielding a maximum annual refundable payment of $800,000. To target small and medium-sized businesses, the grant phases out incrementally for corporations with between $10,000,000 and $50,000,000 in prior-year taxable capital, and firms with $50,000,000 or more in taxable capital—as well as partnerships, trusts, and individuals—are ineligible. Eligible corporations claim the grant by filing AT1 Schedule 29 (Alberta Innovation Employment Grant, Form AT29) alongside Form AT4970 (Listing of Innovation Employment Grant Projects Carried Out in Alberta) and AT1 Schedule 16 (Form AT238) within 15 months after the corporation's AT1 filing due date. Payments are processed by TRA once qualifying expenses have been verified by the CRA and confirmed to have been undertaken in Alberta, and any recapture creates or increases Alberta corporate tax otherwise payable.
Integrated Federal-Provincial Stacking Analysis and Strategic Conclusions
Quantitative Modelling of Combined Federal-Provincial Tax Recovery

Because provincial R&D tax credits constitute government assistance under subsection 127(9) of the federal Income Tax Act, the effective combined cash recovery rate is not a simple arithmetic sum of the federal and provincial statutory rates; rather, the provincial credit must first be deducted from the federal qualified expenditure pool before applying the 35% or 15% federal ITC rate.

To illustrate this statutory interaction, consider a qualifying CCPC (or ECPC) in its 2026 taxation year (beginning on or after December 16, 2024) that incurs $1,000,000 of eligible direct SR&ED engineering salaries in Ontario (using the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount method under Regulation 2900(4), assuming no specified employees) as compared to an identical first-year R&D claimant operating in Alberta with a $0 prior two-year base spending level:

body.text: Strategic and Audit Compliance Conclusions

The legislative enactment of Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026, fundamentally re-anchors Canada's competitive position in North American R&D tax policy. By doubling the enhanced 35% expenditure limit to $6 million, extending full refundability to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations, expanding the phase-out corridor to $15 million–$75 million with an elective gross revenue averaging test, and restoring capital and lease expenditure eligibility effective December 16, 2024, Parliament has resolved the historical growth bottlenecks that previously penalized capital-intensive and publicly listed Canadian innovators.

To secure these enhanced fiscal benefits while insulating claims against CRA technical and financial audit adjustments, corporate claimants and tax advisors must align their internal accounting and documentation practices with five core statutory imperatives. First, asset-heavy CCPCs—such as clean-tech hardware manufacturers, biotechnology enterprises, and venture-backed scale-ups whose balance-sheet equity or debt pushes their taxable capital employed in Canada above $15 million—should model and elect the three-year average gross revenue phase-out method on Schedule T2SCH31 to preserve their full $6 million enhanced expenditure limit, while ensuring associated group allocation agreements are timely filed under subsection 127(10.3). Second, before filing the initial Form T661 for a taxation year—at which point the Line 160 overhead election becomes irrevocable under section 37—compute-intensive software and AI enterprises should benchmark their incremental cloud computing and development software spend against 55% of their eligible SR&ED salary base (calculated net of Regulation 2900(7)–(9) specified employee caps and exclusions), electing the Traditional Method whenever actual incremental compute and overhead exceed the 55% notional proxy. Third, for laboratory equipment, prototyping machinery, custom tooling, and dedicated R&D computing hardware acquired on or after December 16, 2024, claimants must maintain contemporaneous usage logs demonstrating that at least 90% (all or substantially all) of operating time is dedicated to domestic SR&ED, and carefully track subsequent commercial conversions or dispositions to prevent unexpected ITC recapture on Schedule T2SCH31. Fourth, engineering and R&D teams must structure their contemporaneous documentation around the five judicial criteria of Northwest Hydraulic as clarified in Jentel Manufacturing and Manning Canning Kitchens, explicitly recording why standard procedures or publicly available solutions failed to resolve the system-level technological uncertainty before experimental hypotheses were formulated and tested. Fifth, corporate tax departments must enforce strict calendar controls to ensure Form T661, Schedule T2SCH31, and provincial filings (such as Ontario claims, Revenu Québec CRIC forms, and Alberta AT1 Schedule 29) are submitted well before the non-extendable 18-month federal statutory bar under subsections 37(11) and 220(2.2) (and the 15-month post-due-date bar in Alberta), while verifying complete accuracy of Part 9 claim preparer disclosures to eliminate joint and several penalty exposure under subsection 162(5.1).
